info.bio:
The Supremes fue un grupo pop y soul estadounidense formado exclusivamente por chicas que interpretó canciones de distintos géneros musicales, desde el doo wop a la psicodelia y la música disco. Se formó en 1961 en la ciudad de Detroit, Sus primeras integrantes fueron Diana Ross, Mary Wilson y Florence Ballard.

Originalmente se llamaban The Primettes, y eran un cuarteto, ya que también contaban con la presencia de Barbara Martin. Con esta formación sólo grabaron un single en la compañía "Lupine" en 1960.

scenes.name: Motown: Supremes y Holland-Dozier-Holland
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Los grupos de Tamla/Motown ocuparon el hueco de los girl groups: Martha and the Vandellas («Heat Wave», «Dancing in the Street», «Nowhere to Run»), Gladys Knight, las Marvelettes, las Velvelettes y, sobre todo, las Supremes, el grupo pop americano de más éxito del momento (seis números 1 en dos años). Tres amigas del proyecto Brewster-Douglass, las «Supremes sin éxitos» hasta «Where Did Our Love Go» (1964): Berry Gordy vio en ellas el caballo de Troya para entrar en el mercado blanco, con los Funk Brothers, la escritura «psicológica» de Holland-Dozier-Holland (playlets femeninos sobre el amor como adicción, música dura contra letras sumisas) y el departamento de Artist Development de Maxine Powell y Cholly Atkins. Su imagen de espectáculo (Copacabana, pelucas) contrastaba con la nueva bohemia rock, como en su incómodo encuentro con unos Beatles fumados. Diana Ross ardía: seis números 1 y aún las trataban como a un grupo cualquiera.

scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

scenes.name: Soul y Motown
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Al otro lado del océano, la alternativa a los grupos británicos fue el heredero del rhythm'n'blues: el soul. El sonido Memphis (Wilson Pickett, Otis Redding, Sam & Dave) nace de bandas instrumentales casi anónimas como Booker T & the MG's; Motown triunfa con el soul melódico y bailable de Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson y el trío Holland-Dozier-Holland («quizá el mayor fenómeno pop de todos los tiempos»); Phil Spector lanza el «blue-eyed soul» con los Righteous Brothers, y James Brown, con su estilo percusivo, inventa el funk.

podcast.title: First Motown Act with Two Number Ones (1964)
podcast.body: With "Baby Love" reaching number one by October 1964, The Supremes became the first act on the Motown label to achieve two number-one singles, signaling their burgeoning dominance in the music industry. "making the Supremes the first motown act to have two number ones."

podcast.title: "The No Hit Supremes" Nickname
podcast.body: Prior to the release of "Where Did Our Love Go," the group was infamously known within Motown as "the No Hit Supremes" due to their string of unsuccessful singles. "up until this record was known in Motown as the No Hit Supremes."

podcast.title: Affair with Barry Gordy and Ethical Scrutiny
podcast.body: Diana Ross's affair with Motown head Barry Gordy has been a recurring point of criticism, with accusations that she used it to further her ambitions. The narrative highlights that such criticism is often misogynistic and suggests that if there was ethical misconduct in the relationship between a powerful, older, married employer and his much younger employee, the primary fault is unlikely to lie with Ross. "criticises her for having affairs with prominent people at Motown, most notably Barry Gordy, and accuses her of doing this in order to further her own ambitions."

podcast.body: The Primettes successfully secured an audition with Motown head Barry Gordy, who offered encouragement but advised them to return after completing their schooling. "the girls did indeed audition for Barry Gordy, who was encouraging, but told them to come back after they had finished school."

podcast.title: Audition for Smokey Robinson and Marvin Tarplan's Departure
podcast.body: During their audition for Smokey Robinson, he was largely unimpressed by The Primettes' vocals but highly regarded their guitarist, Marvin Tarplan. Robinson then struck a deal: he would secure a Motown audition for the girls if he could borrow Tarplan for an upcoming Miracles tour, a "temporary" arrangement that ultimately lasted 50 years. "Robinson wasn't hugely impressed, except with their guitarist, so Robinson made a deal with them."

podcast.title: Barbara Martin's Departure and Transition to Trio
podcast.body: Barbara Martin, who had recorded material with The Supremes that was later released, left the group due to pregnancy. Following her departure, the remaining three members—Diana Ross, Mary Wilson, and Florence Ballard—decided to continue as a trio. "she became pregnant and decided to leave the group. Having decided that they clearly couldn't keep a fourth single around, the other three decided to continue on as a trio."

podcast.body: From the outset, Barry Gordy demonstrated a primary interest in Diana Ross as an individual star, rather than The Supremes as a collective group. While other members initially took lead on album tracks, singles were generally reserved for Diana, with one notable exception. "he was only interested in Diana Russ as an individual, though at least at first all the members would get to take lead vocals on album tracks, though the singles would be safe for Diana, with one exception."

podcast.title: Barry Gordy's Vision for "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: Despite the group's and producers' unhappiness with the recording session for "Where Did Our Love Go," Barry Gordy, after hearing the playback, was immediately convinced it would be a hit. His enthusiasm was pivotal, and he declared, "cheer up everybody, from now on you're the big hit Supremes," initiating a massive promotional push for the song. "Gordy, much to Ross's shock, was convinced it was a hit, and said to them, cheer up everybody, from now on you're the big hit Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Betty McGlown's Departure
podcast.body: Betty McGlown, who had always been less committed to The Primettes than the other members, decided to leave the group to get married, leading to her quick replacement by Barbara Martin. "Betty decided to leave the group to get married."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Betty McGlown's Lack of Commitment
podcast.body: Betty McGlown was the least committed member of the original group, participating primarily as a favor to her boyfriend, Paul Williams of The Primes. "Betty was the least interested in being in a group she was just doing it as a favour for her boyfriend."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Breakthrough with Freddie Gohrmann and Brian Holland
podcast.body: The Primettes' persistence at Motown's studio paid off when Freddie Gohrmann, a postman and songwriter, was working on a song with Brian Holland. Gohrmann suggested the girls try out the song with harmonies, and the positive result led to Barry Gordy's involvement in tinkering with the song and co-producing the session. "Gohrmann suggested they try the song out to see what it sounded like with harmonies, and the result was good enough that Holland and Gohrmann called in Gordy, who tinkered with the song to get his name on the credits, and then helped produce the session."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Breakthrough with Holland-Dozier-Holland
podcast.body: The Supremes' fortunes finally turned when they were paired with Holland-Dozier-Holland, who had recently achieved success with The Vandellas. This partnership, driven by Barry Gordy's persistent belief in Diana Ross's star potential, ultimately led to their first bona fide hit. "nothing happened until they were paired with Holland Dozier and Holland, fresh off their success with the Van Dellers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Coerced Recording of "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: The Supremes were compelled to record "Where Did Our Love Go," a song previously rejected by the more established Marvelettes, and were advised by them to avoid it. Unlike other Motown artists, The Supremes, due to their lack of success at the time, had no choice but to record the track despite their strong dislike for it and feeling they were getting "everyone else's leftovers." "the Supremes weren't yet, and didn't have any choice, they were going to record the song whether they liked it or not."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Continued String of Flops and "No Hit Supremes" Nickname
podcast.body: Following "Your Heart Belongs To Me," The Supremes released a series of commercially unsuccessful singles, many described as "truly terrible," that barely scraped the bottom of the Top 100 charts but were not considered hits. This period solidified their nickname as "the No Hit Supremes," as they were often given songs deemed unsuitable for other Motown groups. "The group got the nickname the No Hit Supremes, and tended to get the songs that wouldn't pass muster for all the groups."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Contrasting Vocal Styles and Ambition (Ballard vs. Ross)
podcast.body: Florence Ballard was a natural, passionate singer who deeply moved audiences with seemingly little effort, whereas Diana Ross was a more calculated performer, diligently working to improve her vocals and learn what resonated with audiences, despite Ballard initially believing Ross shouldn't be a lead singer. "Ballard was a natural singer, who sang passionately in a way that apparently blew audiences away with relatively little effort because she was singing from the heart. Ross, on the other hand, was a calculated performer, who was deliberately trying to gain the audience's popularity and was improving with every show as she learned what worked."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Detroit Origins
podcast.body: Like many Motown acts, The Supremes' story begins in Detroit, specifically evolving from an earlier male vocal group called The Primes. "the Supremes starts, like almost every Motown act, in Detroit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Diana Ross's Entry and Early Group Dynamics
podcast.body: While Diana Ross claimed to be singing around the neighborhood, Mary Wilson stated they didn't know her, suggesting Jenkins brought her in. The group's members, although from the same area, were assembled by a third party rather than forming organically as friends, a dynamic that significantly impacted their relationships over time. "this wasn't a group that came together as friends, but people who were put together by a third party."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Diana Ross's Name Spelling
podcast.body: Diana Ross was initially known by the spelling "Diane" on her birth certificate, which she attributes to a misspelling by the person filling out the document. She asserts her parents always intended her name to be "Diana," the spelling she has consistently used for many decades since. "she says herself that her parents always intended to name her Diana, and the person filling in the birth certificate misspelled it, and she's used Diana for many decades now."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Diana Ross's Reluctance and Studio Behavior during "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: Diana Ross expressed strong displeasure about singing "Where Did Our Love Go," viewing it as a "terrible song" and "everyone else's leftovers." She resisted Eddie Holland's coaching on phrasing and threatened to call Barry Gordy. She performed the lead vocal with minimal emotion, "glaring daggers at the producers," and stormed off immediately after finishing her take. "She sang through her lead, putting this little emotion as she could into her voice, while glaring daggers at the producers, before storming off as soon as she completed the take they wanted, complaining about being given everyone else's leftovers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Early Lack of Success and Internal Derision
podcast.body: Despite being signed before The Marvelettes, The Supremes struggled for several years, releasing two singles without significant success. They were often regarded as "a joke among the Motown staff," with a common belief that Barry Gordy's attraction to Diane Ross, rather than the group's talent, was the primary reason for their signing. "But the Supremes, as they were renamed, wouldn't become successful for several years, and were generally regarded as a joke among the Motown staff, who thought, not entirely without reason, that they had been signed more because Barry Gordy was attracted to Diane Ross, one of the members of the group, than because of any talent they had."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Early Repertoire and Lead Vocal Distribution
podcast.body: The Primettes' early acts frequently featured songs like Ray Charles's "Night Time is the Right Time," "The Twist," and "There Goes My Baby." While all members took lead vocals on stage, Florence Ballard was considered the primary lead. "That would become a staple of the girls' early acts. Along with the twist, and there goes my baby."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Early Reputation of Diana Ross
podcast.body: Before joining The Primettes, Diana Ross had an established reputation among those involved in Detroit's talent shows, with friends like Melvin Franklin (from The Distants) praising her singing abilities. This early recognition likely played a role in Jenkins inviting her to the group. "Ross was probably introduced to the group, because she already had a reputation among the people who were playing Detroit's talent shows."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: First Motown Contact via Diana Ross and Smokey Robinson
podcast.body: The Primettes' initial significant contact with Motown Records was facilitated by Diana Ross, who leveraged her prior friendship and adolescent crush on Smokey Robinson. Knowing Robinson was recording for Motown, Ross reached out, leading him to suggest an audition for her group, with the promise of an introduction to Barry Gordy if successful. "their first real contact with Motown came through Ross."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Florence Ballard as Early Group Leader
podcast.body: In the early stages of The Primettes, Florence Ballard was unequivocally the group's leader, possessing the most outspoken personality and the strongest voice. She was the first to sing out during auditions, performing Ray Charles's "Night Time is the Right Time." "Florence Ballard was the leading with a group. She had the most outspoken personality and also had the best voice."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Florence Ballard's Last Lead Vocal on a Single
podcast.body: Florence Ballard sang lead on The Supremes' second single, "Butter Pop Corn." However, the song was a commercial failure, proving "no more successful than I want to go," and marked the final occasion Florence Ballard would ever sing lead on a Supremes single. "that would be the last time Florence Ballard ever got to sing lead on a Supremes single."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Florence Ballard's Popularity and Support
podcast.body: Florence Ballard, a member of The Supremes, was highly popular among Motown staff, known for her helpful and friendly nature. She assisted Gladys Horton in crafting her lead vocal performance for "Please Mr. Postman," showcasing inter-group collaboration despite The Supremes' then-unsuccessful status. "One of the girls, though, Florence Ballard, was very popular at Motown, and was generally regarded as being helpful and friendly. She worked with Gladys on her lead vocal part, and helped her craft her performance."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Florence Ballard's Role in Name Selection
podcast.body: While details are disputed, the consensus is that Florence Ballard selected the name "The Supremes" from a short list. Disagreements persist over whether the list was generated by group members or Janie Bradford, and whether Ballard's choice was deliberate or random. "it seems to be the consensus that Ballard did pick the name from a short list."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Florence Ballard's Traumatic Experience
podcast.body: Florence Ballard endured a devastating experience when she was raped by an acquaintance, leading to profound and lifelong trauma. This event left her unable to trust anyone, including her friends, and resulted in what would now be diagnosed as post-traumatic stress disorder, significantly influencing her later interactions and conflicts within the group, particularly with Diana Ross. "Florence Ballard was raped by an acquaintance. This traumatized Ballard deeply, and from this point on she became unable to trust anyone, even her friends."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Followers of The Shirelles' Template
podcast.body: The Supremes are listed as one of the prominent girl groups that followed in the footsteps of The Shirelles, who set the template for the booming girl group sound of the 1960s. "The Supremes, the Marvelettes, the crystals, the Ronettes, and the rest, all were following in the Chirrells footsteps."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Formation as The Primettes
podcast.body: Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard were part of The Primettes, a group that named themselves after The Primes (who later became The Temptations). The Primettes later changed their name and became The Supremes. "Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard, who would go on to form the Supremes"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Formation of The Primettes
podcast.body: The formation of The Primettes by Milton Jenkins involved various approaches, including stopping girls in their housing project. Betty McGlown was chosen due to her relationship with Paul Williams of The Primes, while Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard, who knew each other and were strong singers, joined together, with Ballard initially taking the role of the group's leader. "Betty McGlown was dating Paul Williams, so she was an obvious choice. Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard knew each other and were good singers, especially Ballard, and they joined together, with Ballard becoming the new group's leader."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Internal Strife and Rumors of Diana Ross's Solo Ambitions
podcast.body: Despite their commercial success, significant internal conflict began to emerge within The Supremes, even during the Dick Clark tour. Rumors circulated about Diana Ross's desire for a solo career and discussions arose about her potential efforts to force Florence Ballard out of the group. "Even on the Dick Clark tour bus, there were rumours that Diana Ross wanted a solo career, and there was talk of her forcing Florence Ballard out of the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Late 60s Dominance
podcast.body: The Supremes, described as Motown superstars, dominated the late 1960s, after which the initial girl group era was considered to have passed into history. "After Motown superstars, the Supremes dominated the late 60s, the Girl Group era passed into history."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Be My Baby-Baby-Baby Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Leading Girl Group in Chart History
podcast.body: Unsurprisingly, Billboard ranks The Supremes as the leading girl group in chart history, ahead of TLC, Destiny's Child, and The Pointer Sisters. "Billboard ranks the pointer sisters as the fourth biggest girl group in chart history, after in third place Destiny's Child, in second place TLC, and leading the pack unsurprisingly the Supremes."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Yes We Can Can Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Management Transition and Self-Reliance
podcast.body: After their initial manager, Milton Jenkins, left management following a hospital stay, The Primettes began to manage themselves, taking over their own affairs. "Franklin dropped out of management, he spent some time in hospital, and after getting out he just never got back in touch with the girls, and the primates took over looking after themselves."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Marvin Tarplan - The Primettes' Guitarist
podcast.body: Marvin Tarplan was a unique fifth member of The Primettes, who, despite not singing, played guitar, making them one of the few vocal groups in Detroit at the time to have their own instrumental accompaniment. "Marvin Tarplan, who didn't sing but in play guitar, which made them one of the few vocal groups in the city, who had their own accompaniment."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Mary Wilson as Peacemaker
podcast.body: Mary Wilson consistently acted as the group's peacemaker, adept at resolving conflicts and mediating disputes between Florence Ballard and Diana Ross due to her strong aversion to conflict. "Mary Wilson was always the peacemaker, someone who was so conflict diverse, she would find a way to get Florence and Diana to stop fracking no matter what."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Mary Wilson's Legacy and Passing
podcast.body: Mary Wilson was the only member of The Supremes to remain with the group from its inception until its split in 1977. Despite The Supremes being the second most commercially successful group of the 1960s after The Beatles, Wilson was considered "under rewarded" in life, and her recent passing was "under reported." "Mary Wilson, the only member of the Supremes who stayed with the group from the beginning right through to their split in 1977."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Misogynistic Portrayal in Biographies
podcast.body: Diana Ross has faced significant criticism, often rooted in misogyny, from colleagues and biographers. A male biographer, for instance, described her as looking "emaciated and vacant" (noting her struggle with anorexia), compared her face to E.T., and suggested she used her sexuality to advance her career, particularly in criticisms regarding her affair with Barry Gordy. "almost all the negative things said about her have a deep undercurrent of misogyny."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Most Successful Girl Group
podcast.body: The Supremes are recognized as the most successful girl group in chart history, having achieved 12 number one hits. Their first chart-topper and breakthrough hit was "Where Did Our Love Go," which also won the 1964 Song of the Summer title. "the breakthrough hit for the most successful girl group in chart history. The first of 12 number ones for the Supremes."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Song(s) of the Summer Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Most Successful Vocal Group of the 60s
podcast.body: The Supremes became the most successful vocal group of the 1960s, also recognized as the most important act from Motown. In terms of chart success, they were surpassed only by The Beatles and Elvis during that decade. "The group who have become the most successful vocal group of the 60s."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Name Change: The Primettes to The Supremes
podcast.body: The group officially changed its name from The Primettes to The Supremes with the release of their first single under the new moniker. The origin of the name was contentious, leading to later legal disputes where Florence Ballard claimed intellectual property rights as the one who chose it. "the primates had now become the Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Persistence and Strategy to Join Motown
podcast.body: Despite facing multiple setbacks, including Florence Ballard's trauma and their manager's imprisonment, The Primettes demonstrated ambition and determination to join Motown. They proactively frequented Hitsville U.S.A., performing minor session work like handclaps and backing vocals, effectively immersing themselves in the studio environment until they gained an opportunity. "the primates were ambitious, and they decided that they were going to force their way into Motown where the very good he wanted them or not."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Rapid Ascent to Number One on Dick Clark Tour
podcast.body: Upon the release of "Where Did Our Love Go" in June, The Supremes were the opening act at the bottom of the bill on Dick Clark's Caravan of Stars tour, performing alongside over a dozen other acts. Their single rapidly ascended the charts, reaching number one by the tour's conclusion. "By the end of the tour, their record was at number one in the chart."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Rise and Impact
podcast.body: The rise of The Supremes within Motown led to other groups, like The Marvelettes and The Van Dellers, becoming less important to the label. "the rise of the Supremes... meant that like the Marvelettes before them, the Van Della's became less important to Motown."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Session Work with Other Labels
podcast.body: Despite Barry Gordy's initial deferral, Motown producers Richard Marvis and Robert Bateman chose not to wait, instead becoming The Primettes' managers and securing them session work on other labels, including early recordings for future soul legends like Wilson Pickett. "Marvis became their major, and they started getting session work on early recordings by future soul legends, like Wilson Pickett."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Spontaneous "Baby Baby" Backing Vocals for "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: During the recording of "Where Did Our Love Go," the other two Supremes struggled with the difficult backing vocal parts devised by Lamont Dozier, exacerbated by their poor mood and Mary Wilson's disappointment. A frustrated Dozier eventually instructed them to simply sing "baby baby" when prompted, which became the iconic backing vocal. "frustrated Dozier told them to just sing baby baby when he pointed, and they went with that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Struggles with Chart Success (Two-Year Period)
podcast.body: For two years, The Supremes continued to struggle with chart success, consistently being surpassed by other Motown acts like The Marvelettes and The Vandellas, who had signed after them but achieved hits sooner. Despite various producers, including Lamont Dozier, Brian Holland, Barry Gordy, and Smokey Robinson, attempting to record with them, their singles rarely charted above the bottom of the Top 100. "This sort of thing continued for two years, with the Supremes now being passed in chart success, not only by the Marvelettes, but also by the Van Dellers."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Studio Conflict and Lead Vocal Dispute for "Where Did Our Love Go"
podcast.body: The recording session for "Where Did Our Love Go" was marked by significant tension, largely due to a dispute over the lead vocalist. Mary Wilson was initially told she would sing lead, but Barry Gordy's directive (or a producer's insistence, accounts vary) shifted lead duties to Diana Ross, devastating Wilson and annoying Ross, who disliked the song and its low key. "Mary was devastated, while Ross was annoyed that she was having to sing what she thought was a terrible song, in a key that was much lower than she was used to."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes

podcast.title: Talent Contest Rivals
podcast.body: As The Primettes, they developed a rivalry with The Delphiys (Martha Reeves' group) and The Primes, often taking turns winning amateur night talent contests. "developed a rivalry with two other groups. The Primes, who would later go on to be the Temptations and the Primette, who would name themselves after the Primes, but later became the Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 111: "Heat Wave" by Martha and the Vandellas

podcast.title: Touring as The Marvelettes Substitute
podcast.body: At one point, when Wonder Young of The Marvelettes was pregnant, Florence Ballard replaced her on tour to fulfill a contractual obligation for five Marvelettes. This highlights the fluidity of Motown's touring lineups and the good relations between Florence and the Marvelettes. "At one point when Wonder had been pregnant, Motown had replaced him on the road with Florence Ballard from the Supremes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 93: "Please Mr. Postman" by the Marvelettes

podcast.title: Transition from Backing Group to Standalone Act
podcast.body: Initially formed as a potential backing group for The Primes, Milton Jenkins soon recognized the potential of The Primettes as a distinct vocal group in their own right. "Jenkins soon realised that this group could be better used as a group in their own right, rather than merely as backing vocalists for the primes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 116: "Where Did Our Love Go?" by The Supremes
